content.summary: Welcome to your reading mission for Unit 7. In this lesson, you will read about future plans, schedules, and predictions. You will learn how to identify different future verb forms and understand how people talk about upcoming events in everyday English.

linguisticTarget.grammar: Present simple for timetables, be going to for intentions, will for predictions, and present continuous for personal arrangements.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Words and phrases related to organizing events, making predictions, and discussing intentions.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Skimming the passage for general understanding and scanning for specific future time expressions.

learningObjectives: Understand the main ideas of short B1 texts about future plans and events.
Locate specific details such as times, dates, and organized arrangements.
Recognize grammar patterns related to future predictions and scheduled events.

contextWarmup.prompt: Which future form do we use when we talk about a fixed timetable, like a train departure or a film start time?
contextWarmup.explanation: We use the Present Simple tense for fixed timetables and schedules that do not change easily.

rules: Use the Present Simple for scheduled events and timetables in the future.
Use be going to for personal plans, intentions, and decisions made before speaking.
Use will and won't for general predictions, promises, and spontaneous decisions.

commonTrap.explanation: Learners often use will for personal plans they have already decided on, instead of using be going to.
commonTrap.wrong: I will visit my grandmother this weekend. (When it is already arranged)
commonTrap.correct: I am going to visit my grandmother this weekend. (For established plans and intentions)

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Future Fun and Conditional Plans

content.summary: Practical guide on writing future plans, predictions, and conditional sentences using if, when, and unless.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: First Conditional Structure
blueprintItems.formula: If / When / Unless + Present Simple, Future Simple (will / won't)
blueprintItems.example: If it rains tomorrow, we will stay at home and watch a film.

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: Scheduled Future and Intentions
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + Present Simple (for schedules) OR be going to (for plans)
blueprintItems.example: The train leaves at six o'clock, and I am going to pack my bag tonight.

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: Agreement with So and Neither
blueprintItems.example: I love planning future trips. So do I.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use a comma after the conditional clause when it comes at the beginning of the sentence.
mechanicsRules.badExample: If you finish your homework early you can join us.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: If you finish your homework early, you can join us.
mechanicsRules.why: A comma separates the dependent 'if' clause from the main clause for clarity.

mechanicsRules.rule: Do not use 'will' directly after if, when, or unless in the conditional clause.
mechanicsRules.badExample: If she will arrive on time, we will start the meeting.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: If she arrives on time, we will start the meeting.
mechanicsRules.why: The conditional clause requires the present simple tense, while the main clause takes future simple.

mechanicsRules.rule: Always capitalize the pronoun 'I' and the first letter of every new sentence.
mechanicsRules.badExample: unless you hurry, i will leave without you.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: Unless you hurry, I will leave without you.
mechanicsRules.why: Proper sentence boundaries and personal pronouns require standard English capitalization.

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: Future Fun: First Conditional with If, When & Unless

content.summary: Mastering spoken English for B1 requires clear articulation of conditional clauses, correct stress patterns in future predictions, and natural intonation when negotiating arrangements or making plans.
content.audioGuidance: Pay close attention to sentence stress. In first conditional sentences, stress the main verbs and the modal will. Pause briefly between the if clause and the main clause.

pillars.name: Clause Linking
pillars.explanation: When speaking sentences with if, when, or unless, link the final consonant of the conjunction to the vowel sound of the next word.

pillars.name: Future Modal Reduction
pillars.target: Natural reduction of will to ll
pillars.explanation: Native speakers typically contract will to ll in speech, saying I will as I'll and you will as you'll.

pillars.name: Intonation in Negotiations
pillars.target: Rising intonation for options, falling for decisions
pillars.explanation: Use rising intonation when proposing alternatives and falling intonation when confirming a final arrangement.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: The stress moves depending on the word form, shifting to the second syllable in both words.
The primary stress remains on the second syllable for both the verb and noun forms.
Both the base verb and the past participle maintain stress on the final syllable.
Stress shifts slightly from the second syllable of the noun to the second syllable of the verb.
